saint_pick.name: Winifred
saint_pick.selection_reason: Winifred's story is vivid and moving: a Welsh virgin beheaded by Prince Caradog for refusing him, then restored to life by her uncle St Beuno, with a healing spring rising where her head fell. It is documented in a 12th-century vita and continues in the living pilgrimage at Holywell, made a National Shrine in November 2023. She is lesser-known than a household-name saint, and Wales is a fresh region and era after the recent Gaul, Pannonia and Iberia entries.
saint_pick.catholic_veneration: Canonized pre-congregation virgin martyr listed in the Roman Martyrology on 3 November. She is celebrated in Wales and in the Archdiocese of Cardiff and Diocese of Wrexham, and St Winefride's Well at Holywell is the National Shrine of England and Wales.

script.summary: According to legend, Saint Winifred, a seventh-century Welsh noblewoman, refused a suitor, was restored to life through Saint Beuno, and later served as abbess at Gwytherin, while the spring at Holywell remains a national shrine.

claims.claim: Winifred (Welsh: Gwenffrewi) was a Welsh virgin martyr of the 7th century.
According to legend, she was the daughter of a chieftain of Tegeingl, Tyfid ap Eiludd.
According to legend, her suitor Caradog was enraged when she decided to become a nun and, when she refused his advances, decapitated her.
A healing spring appeared where her head fell.
Her head was rejoined to her body through the efforts of Saint Beuno, a relative of her mother, and she was restored to life.
Tradition holds that Beuno promised that whoever asked a benefit of God on that spot in Winifred's name would obtain the grace if it was for the good of his soul.
After eight years at Holywell she received an inspiration to leave, went inland to Gwytherin, and became a nun and abbess there.
An 8th-century oak reliquary of Winifred was identified after pieces were found in 1991, which is evidence of an early cult.
St Winefride's Well at Holywell, Flintshire, is a pilgrimage site granted National Shrine status for England and Wales in November 2023.
Winifred is commemorated on 3 November in the liturgical calendar for Wales.

issues: saint.martyr was false, but the source calls her a 'virgin martyr' and 'martyr saint' (also an 'honorary martyr' in iconography), and claim 1 says martyr. Set to true.
'Who' beat stated the chieftain parentage as plain fact, but the source gives it only as legend. Added 'by tradition'.

'Turn' beat stated the move to Gwytherin and the abbess role as fact, but the source gives them as legend (and says she became a nun and abbess there 'later'). Added 'Tradition says' and kept the length within 125-145 words (now about 143).
Hook scene described Beuno as a 'saintly bishop', but the sources never call him a bishop. Changed to 'saintly monk'.

caption_hook said the pilgrimage 'has never stopped', which the sources do not support. The Shrewsbury shrine was destroyed in 1540 and the sources only say Holywell is now a pilgrimage site. Reworded.
